section_summary: This section contains embassy telegrams and summaries of monitored Japanese broadcasts about wartime production, labor, transport, agriculture, rationing, and administration across Japanese-occupied Asia. It also includes transmission notes, a withdrawn-item notice, a Navy request for broadcast copies, and a report assessing Japanese radio propaganda aimed at Australia.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Moscow telegram no. 126 summarizing Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.about: Summarizes December 1942 and January 1943 Japanese broadcasts for the Board of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: The broadcasts describe agriculture, transport, industrial output, rationing, health measures, and reconstruction in Japan, Manchukuo, and occupied territories. Topics include Philippine railways and cotton, Manchukuo labor and agricultural plans, rubber controls, and appeals for greater production.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram no. 128, section one
subfiles.about: Reports monitored Japanese broadcasts from January 7–18.
subfiles.summary: The broadcasts concern trade agreements, Chinese and Manchukuo production, railways, postal service, research, and food and commodity controls. They also describe Japanese appeals to conserve coal and consumer goods and acknowledge maritime transport difficulties.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram no. 128, section two
subfiles.about: Reports broadcasts on Manchukuo labor mobilization and Manila–Shanghai trade.
subfiles.summary: A Manchukuo broadcast urges greater mining labor, farm mechanization, recruitment in North China, and women's farm work. Another announces an exchange of Philippine sugar and jute for goods from Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Moscow telegram no. 128
subfiles.about: Paraphrases both sections of telegram no. 128 for the Board of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate account covers January broadcasts about trade, industrial output, transport, postal services, health research, and rationing throughout Japanese-controlled Asia. It gives extended attention to Manchukuo's need for coal and iron workers, including proposed peasant mine work and women's farm labor.

subfiles.title: Restricted-item withdrawal notice
subfiles.about: Records the withdrawal of file item 894.76/119 because access is restricted.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the withdrawn item and cites restricted information.

subfiles.title: Kuibyshev telegram no. 260 on Japanese radio stations
subfiles.about: Reports a pending request for Japanese station frequencies and schedules audible in the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office has not replied; Moscow hopes to expand monitoring reports when staffing improves.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Kuibyshev telegram no. 260
subfiles.about: Restates the embassy's unanswered request for Japanese broadcast frequencies and schedules.
subfiles.summary: Moscow plans fuller reporting after its personnel shortage eases.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram no. 193, section one
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese broadcasts on radio receivers, industry, trade, cotton, and language policy.
subfiles.summary: Items include compulsory alteration of Philippine radio sets, power station plans, trade negotiations, Java cotton and railway work, and the promotion of Japanese as a regional common language.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram no. 193, section two
subfiles.about: Summarizes broadcasts about Manchukuo labor and agriculture and occupied-area production.
subfiles.summary: The broadcasts discuss Korean road building, Manchukuo food transport, mining labor, plague control, identity certificates, and ration cards. They also cover Shanghai machine tools, oil claims, Java and Sumatra crops, and Javanese administrative appointments.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram no. 193, section three
subfiles.about: Reports broadcasts on war materials, Philippine labor, cotton, and Singapore.
subfiles.summary: Items concern Manchukuo cast iron, repaired Philippine automobile facilities, Japanese military donations, Singapore's naval base, Philippine employment and cotton, forest conservation, and suspended labor protections.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Moscow telegram no. 193
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the three sections of telegram no. 193 for the Board of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate account compiles broadcasts from December 1942 through February 1943 about radio controls, trade, language policy, labor, agriculture, transport, and industrial production. It includes detailed claims about Manchukuo mobilization and production, cultivation in Java and Sumatra, and employment and administration in the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Chungking telegram no. 541, section one
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese monitoring of Japanese broadcasts on expanded cotton cultivation.
subfiles.summary: The section gives Japanese targets and estimates for cotton acreage and output in the Philippines, Burma, and Sumatra, including planned five-year expansion and new processing facilities.

subfiles.title: Chungking telegram no. 541, section two
subfiles.about: Continues the cotton survey across Japanese-controlled Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: The section gives cotton plans or estimates for Java, Celebes, the Lesser Sunda Islands, French Indochina, and Thailand, including proposed seed imports and research.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to monitored Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.about: Points to an original paper transmitting copies of monitored Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to file 103.917/1639.

subfiles.title: Transcripts of Japanese broadcasts, December 23–January 8
subfiles.from: Llewellyn E. Thompson Jr., American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Forwards Soviet-monitored broadcast transcripts for the Board of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the transcripts and notes that an economic summary was sent on February 27.

subfiles.title: Summaries of Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.about: Transmits summaries referenced in telegram no. 126.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the broadcast summaries requested by the Board of Economic Warfare.

subfiles.title: Monitored Japanese broadcasts, December 30–February 15
subfiles.from: William H. Standley, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.about: Transmits Soviet-supplied broadcast transcripts following telegram no. 193.
subfiles.summary: Forwards transcripts covering December 30, 1942, through February 15, 1943.

subfiles.title: Request for Japanese domestic radio propaganda copies
subfiles.from: M. Zacharias, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: Requests copies of Japanese domestic radio propaganda sent by the Moscow embassy.
subfiles.summary: Asks that Naval Intelligence receive the broadcast copies.

subfiles.title: Manchuria: foreign recognition of Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Extracts a Radio Tokyo claim about diplomatic recognition of Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Reports Tokyo's claim that fifteen countries recognize Manchukuo, with Soviet and Vatican de facto recognition.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese broadcasts to the United States
subfiles.about: Points to an original file entry transmitting Japanese broadcasts aimed at the United States.
subfiles.summary: Directs readers to file 894.20200/10.

subfiles.title: Objectives, Character and Effect of Japanese Propaganda Directed to Australia
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Consul General, Melbourne
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese shortwave propaganda directed at Australia and assesses its effect.
subfiles.summary: Dickover describes broadcasts from Tokyo and Japanese-controlled stations that urged Australia to leave the war and join the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. He groups their themes around military threats, alleged Allied weakness and disunity, Australian shortages, and promised economic gains. He judges most broadcasts ineffective, but says Japanese claims about Allied sea and air losses create some doubt because Australian newspapers publish them.
